passage:
I was on the park bench when I saw Himani, the nursery helper, at the gate with a four-year-old who would not put on his shoes. Other adults would have called from across the grass. Himani walked over, crouched until her face was level with his, and said quietly, "Shoes on. Then swing."
That was all. The boy looked at her for a moment, then sat on the step and pushed his foot in. Himani held the other shoe. She did not add reasons or a lecture, and she did not hurry him. When the second strap was fastened, he ran to the swing.
— Avni, park regular

qa.q: What did Himani say when she crouched beside the child at the gate?
qa.a: Himani said, "Shoes on. Then swing."

qa.q: What might Himani have been feeling while she crouched and waited?
qa.a: Himani seems calm and patient, since her voice was quiet and she did not hurry the boy. Avni can only judge from what was visible.

qa.q: What did Himani do that worked better than calling from across the grass?
qa.a: She crouched to eye level and gave one short instruction, then waited. There was no long explanation, so the boy could act at once.

qa.q: What might it have been like for the boy to see Himani's face at his level?
qa.a: It probably felt safe and clear, because he could see her face and hear one simple thing. He sat down and put on his shoe without a fight.

grounding: An adult crouches to eye level, gives one simple instruction and waits, and the young child listens, as seen by someone in the park.

passage:
Monday. Sabina's mother Leela stood at the kitchen door shouting, "Sabina, it is time for your bath, and we have to go early tomorrow and the water is getting cold and if you don't come now..." Sabina kept stacking blocks and did not look up.
Tuesday. Leela knelt beside the tower, eyes level with Sabina's. "Bath time. Two more blocks, then we go." Sabina placed two blocks and took Leela's hand.
Friday. Leela only had to crouch and say, "Bath time." Sabina put down the last block by herself and reached up to be carried, still holding one block in a fist.

qa.q: Which day did Leela kneel beside the tower of blocks?
qa.a: Leela knelt beside the tower on Tuesday.

qa.q: What might Leela have been feeling on Monday while shouting from the kitchen door?
qa.a: Leela was probably hurried and frustrated, since the long list of reasons ran on and Sabina did not look up. The kneeling on Tuesday shows a calmer try.

qa.q: What did Leela change on Tuesday, and how did it help?
qa.a: Leela knelt to Sabina's eye level and gave one short instruction with a small choice of two more blocks. Sabina placed them and took Leela's hand.

qa.q: How might Sabina see the difference between Monday and Tuesday?
qa.a: On Monday Sabina heard a long, rushed stream of words and kept stacking. On Tuesday Sabina saw a face and heard one clear idea, so listening was easy.

grounding: An adult crouches, gives one simple instruction and waits, and a child who ignored a long explanation on the first day listens over three days.

passage:
The platform at Nagpur station was packed, and the train was pulling in with a long, loud horn. Five-year-old Yamini was hopping about, pointing at a balloon seller.
Chetan's first thought was to shout a long list: stay close, don't run, the train is coming, hold the bag. Instead he crouched down until his face was level with hers, put a hand on her shoulder, and said calmly, "Yamini. Hold my hand."
Then he waited.
Yamini looked at him, then at the train, and slid her small hand into his.
"Good," he said. They stepped on together.

qa.q: What was Yamini pointing at on the platform?
qa.a: Yamini was pointing at a balloon seller.

qa.q: Why might Yamini have taken Chetan's hand at once?
qa.a: She likely felt calm and safe because he came down to her eye level and spoke one clear instruction instead of shouting.

qa.q: Which choice worked, and why?
qa.a: Crouching, giving one short instruction and waiting worked better than a long list, which Yamini could not have followed in the noise.

qa.q: What would change if Chetan had shouted a list from above?
qa.a: Yamini might have felt confused or scared by the noise and the words, and might not have listened in time.

grounding: An adult crouches to a child's eye level, gives one short calm instruction and waits, and the child listens.

passage:
It was past bedtime in the Kochi flat, and building blocks covered the floor. Harsha, five, was still stacking.
Jomon had already said it three times from the doorway: "Harsha, it's late, put everything away, brush your teeth, we have school tomorrow, come on." Harsha didn't even look up.
So Jomon walked over and knelt beside him. He waited until Harsha looked at him.
"Blocks in the box," he said softly, and held out the box.
Harsha dropped in one block, then another. "Can I keep the tower?"
"Tower can stay on the shelf."
Harsha carried it carefully, then put the rest away.

qa.q: How many times had Jomon called from the doorway?
qa.a: Jomon had already said it three times from the doorway.

qa.q: What was Harsha likely feeling when he asked to keep the tower?
qa.a: Harsha likely felt calmer and willing, and a little worried about losing the tower he had built.

qa.q: What went differently the fourth time, and why did it work?
qa.a: Jomon knelt, waited for eye contact and gave one concrete instruction with the box ready, so Harsha knew exactly what to do.

qa.q: How did the long doorway instructions seem to Harsha?
qa.a: They seemed like background noise to Harsha, too many words from far away, so he didn't even look up.

grounding: An adult kneels, waits for eye contact and gives one short instruction, and the child listens after long calls failed.

passage:
"Tenzin, shoes, bag, water bottle, and then we have to—"
"Mama, look! A snail!"
"Tenzin, we'll be late. I told you, shoes, bag, water—"
"It has a house on its back!"
Trisha stopped. She put down her keys and crouched on the doormat so her eyes met Tenzin's.
"Tenzin. Shoes on."
"Now?"
"Now." She waited, quiet.
Tenzin pulled on one shoe, then the other. "Can the snail come?"
"The snail stays in the garden. You can say bye."
"Bye, snail."
"Good. Now bag."
"Bag!"

qa.q: What did Tenzin find at the door?
qa.a: Tenzin found a snail.

qa.q: What was Trisha feeling before she crouched down?
qa.a: Trisha was stressed and hurried, worried they would be late, repeating a long list.

qa.q: What small step helped Tenzin get ready?
qa.a: Trisha crouched to Tenzin's eye level, gave one instruction at a time and waited quietly.

qa.q: What is it like for Tenzin when Trisha lists many things at once?
qa.a: Tenzin is too excited about the snail to take in a long list, so the words slip past.

grounding: A parent crouches, gives one simple instruction and waits, and the child listens instead of ignoring a long list.

passage: Observation note, Sunflower room, Tuesday, 11:20. Kashish was running laps around the art table with a glue stick, ignoring three calls to sit. Nirmala, our new assistant, walked over, crouched to eye level and waited until Kashish stopped. Then, calmly: "Glue stick on the tray." Just that. Kashish looked at her, looked at the tray, and put it down. Nirmala smiled. "Thank you. Now chair." Kashish sat. Ten minutes earlier I had heard a long explanation about glue and carpets that got nowhere. I will share this with the whole team at Friday's meeting.

qa.q: What was Kashish running around the art table with?
qa.a: A glue stick.

qa.q: Why did Nirmala wait until Kashish stopped before speaking?
qa.a: Nirmala seemed calm and patient, wanting Kashish's attention first so that one short instruction would land.

qa.q: What will the note-writer share on Friday, and why?
qa.a: How crouching, waiting and giving one short instruction worked where a long explanation about glue and carpets got nowhere 🙂

qa.q: What was it like for Kashish when Nirmala crouched and spoke one short line?
qa.a: Kashish got one clear, calm thing to do at eye level instead of a long talk, which was far easier to take in and follow.

grounding: Shows an adult crouching to eye level, giving one short instruction in a calm voice and waiting, so the child listens.
